headline: Did social media hook kids? A trial begins

sources.title: Meta heads to court in a landmark trial about kids and social media addiction (NPR)
Landmark trial accusing social media companies of addicting children begins (NBC News)
A Meta trial loss could end the social media we know (CNBC)
Meta hooked children on Facebook and Instagram, court hears (video, BBC News)

chunks.text: Were [[likes]], [[endless]] feeds, and [[constant]] notifications designed [[on purpose]] to [[hook]] children? That is the question [[at the heart of]] a huge [[trial]] that began in mid-August in a [[federal court]] in California. Four US states have {{teamed up}} to {{take on}} Meta, the company behind Facebook and Instagram, in one of the biggest tech cases in American history.

verbs.correct: To join others to work together
verbs.wrong: To share the costs of a case
verbs.why: Team up means to join with others so you can work toward a shared goal. Four US states have teamed up to bring this case against Meta together.
Take on means to challenge or fight against someone much bigger or more powerful than you. The states are taking on Meta in one of the largest tech cases in American history.

chunks.text: The case is about app features everyone knows. [[Notifications]] {{pop up}} on the screen [[at all hours]], so young users return [[again and again]]. The [[feed]] never ends, so there is no natural place to stop. Likes and other small rewards {{draw in}} teenagers and keep them [[scrolling]]. Many teens say they cannot {{put down}} the phone, even at dinner or late at night. The states [[argue]] that these [[designs]] were built to hold children's [[attention]], [[whatever the cost]].

verbs.why: Pop up means to appear suddenly on a screen, without any warning. In the case, notifications pop up at all hours and repeatedly interrupt young users.
Draw in means to attract someone's attention and hold it so they keep engaging. Likes and small rewards draw in teenagers and keep them scrolling for hours.
Put down means to stop holding something and set it aside. Many teens say they cannot put down their phone, even at dinner or late at night.

chunks.text: The states want big changes. They ask the court to make Meta {{do away with}} some of these features for young users, and they demand up to 1.4 trillion dollars, one of the largest amounts ever requested in a US court. Meta {{pushes back}} hard against the [[claims]]. The company {{stands by}} its [[record]], saying it has built strong [[protections]] for teens and that the [[demands]] are [[unfair]].

verbs.why: Do away with means to remove something completely so it no longer exists. The states want the court to make Meta do away with certain features built for young users.
Push back means to resist firmly and refuse to accept something. Meta is pushing back hard against the states' claims and denies that its designs are unfair.
Stand by means to keep supporting a decision or statement even when it is challenged. Meta stands by its record on teen safety and insists the demands are unfair.

chunks.text: The trial is expected to {{go on}} for about six weeks, and the whole tech world is watching. A loss could change how social media looks and feels for everyone. An entire [[generation]] has {{grown up}} with likes, notifications, and endless feeds, and courts are only now deciding what that means. In the end, the case may {{come down to}} one question: did the company know its designs could hurt young users?

verbs.why: Go on means to continue happening for a period of time. The trial is expected to go on for about six weeks.
Grow up means to spend the years of your childhood in a particular situation. An entire generation has grown up with likes, notifications, and endless feeds.

verbs.correct: To depend on one main thing
verbs.why: Come down to means that a complicated question really depends on one main point. In the end, the case may come down to whether Meta knew its designs could harm young users.

mainIdea.s: Four US states are taking Meta to trial, saying features like likes and endless feeds were built to hook children. The company denies it and defends its record.
mainIdea.why: The states argue the designs were made to hold children's attention, while Meta pushes back and stands by its protections for teens.

mainIdea.s: A US court has already ruled that Meta must delete its likes and its endless feed for everyone. The company will pay four states 1.4 trillion dollars this fall.
mainIdea.why: Close, but there is no decision yet. The trial just began and is expected to go on for about six weeks.

mainIdea.s: Four US states have launched a free school program that teaches children to use social media safely. Classes will cover likes, feeds, notifications, and screen time.
mainIdea.why: The article is about a court case against Meta, not about a school program for safe social media use.

tf.s: The trial is over, and the court has already made Meta do away with likes
tf.why: The trial began in mid-August and is expected to go on for about six weeks. Nothing has been decided yet.

tf.s: Four US states have teamed up to take on Meta in court
tf.why: Four US states teamed up to take on Meta in a federal court in California.

tf.s: The states demand up to 1.4 trillion dollars
tf.why: They demand up to 1.4 trillion dollars, one of the largest amounts ever requested in a US court.

tf.s: Instead of pushing back, Meta agrees its features were built to hook children
tf.why: Meta pushes back hard. It stands by its record and says it built strong protections for teens.

tf.s: The states say notifications that pop up at all hours help draw in young users
tf.why: Notifications pop up on the screen at all hours, and likes and other small rewards draw in teenagers.

tf.s: The result of the case matters only to Meta
tf.why: A loss could change how social media looks and feels for everyone, and the whole tech world is watching.
